case_study_insert.main_stem: Millbrook Grain Cooperative (MBG) is a cooperative in the grain-milling industry, based on the Canadian prairies and employing a workforce of 72 worker-members. Founded in 1998 by Amina Yusuf, it sells flour to regional bakeries and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MBG plans to invest $840,000 in a new flour mill and grain-silo upgrade, financed by a $500,000 member share issue and $340,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $21, and produces 100,000 units a year. MBG faces grain losses in storage of 6% of intake and absenteeism of 9% among its mill workers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Storage Log — Q4 2025: The mill processed 24,600 sacks of flour last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.8% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 34 to 18 a month. Average delivery to bakeries was 3.4 days. A survey of 640 bakery buyers found 63% would pay $0.25 more for locally milled flour, and 54% check the origin label. Grain loss in storage was 6% of intake. A skills audit shows 14 of 72 worker-members have not completed on-the-job training on the new mill; off-the-job training at the agricultural college costs $640 per member.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Millbrook Grain Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Grain Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.50%, raising the cost of farm and milling finance. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.80 to $14.66 an hour, lifting mill-floor payroll costs. (3) Fertiliser and transport input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on artisan bread grew 3.8%.

questions.question_text: MBG is funding its $840,000 flour mill and grain-silo upgrade with a $500,000 member share issue and $340,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for MBG of the member share issue compared with using more retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share issue raises $500,000 without draining the cooperative's cash reserve, so MBG keeps $340,000 retained profit to absorb the 9.4% rise in fertiliser and transport costs. For a business with fixed costs of $300,000 a year, that liquidity protects the 3.4-day delivery service to regional bakeries while the new mill is built.

Point 2: Raising funds from members spreads the $840,000 cost across the cooperative rather than waiting for profits to accumulate, so Amina Yusuf can upgrade the mill and silos at once. Members who buy shares also have a stake in the business, which fits democratic ownership and can support the 63% of 640 bakery buyers willing to pay $0.25 more for locally milled flour, whereas relying only on retained profit could delay the project.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MBG's financing decision.

questions.question_text: MBG wants to increase sales of locally milled flour to regional bakeries. Consider a regional television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MBG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television: TV would reach many bakeries and households across the prairies and show the new flour mill in action, supporting the 63% of 640 bakery buyers willing to pay $0.25 more. However, airtime is expensive for a cooperative with $300,000 fixed costs and an $840,000 upgrade, and many viewers are not commercial buyers, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local newspaper advertising: Newspapers are cheaper and reach the regional bakery catchment directly, and ads can carry vouchers for first orders. Their limits are declining readership and a static image that cannot convey the 54% of buyers who check the origin label, so they may do little to build the locally milled branding beyond a narrow area.

Social media influencer marketing: Baking influencers can demonstrate the flour in recipes and explain the origin story to a wider audience, with engagement tracked against the 24,600 sacks processed last quarter. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on credible partners, but the cost per reached buyer is low and the content can highlight the fall in complaints from 34 to 18 a month.

Recommendation: MBG should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by small newspaper vouchers for bakery buyers. It targets the segment in the survey, conveys origin that radio and print cannot show fully, and costs far less than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for an $840,000 upgrade; newspapers alone are rejected as too limited to reach bakeries beyond the immediate region.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MBG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MBG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: MBG's absenteeism has reached 9% and grain losses are 6% of intake under its democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for MBG of consultation with its workforce of 72 worker-members.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic consultation lets the 72 worker-members suggest better silo and handling routines, which can reduce the 6% grain loss and the 2.1% defect rate. Being heard raises commitment, so absenteeism should fall from 9%, keeping the new flour mill staffed and protecting the 24,600-sack quarterly output and 3.4-day deliveries.

Point 2: Involvement draws on members' practical knowledge, so small spoilage problems can be flagged early and the 63% of 640 bakery buyers willing to pay $0.25 more receive consistent flour. Higher morale also lowers the cost of retraining the 14 of 72 members without on-the-job training at $640 each, protecting the $21 selling price and contribution while the $840,000 upgrade settles in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MBG's absenteeism, storage losses and expansion.

questions.question_text: MBG must train 14 of 72 worker-members who have not completed on-the-job training on the new mill. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the agricultural college. Which should MBG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the mill is specific to MBG's own equipment and flour standards, costs no fees, and keeps the 14 trainees productive during the 24,600-sack quarter. It can directly reduce the 6% grain loss and the 2.1% defect rate because supervisors correct practice immediately. Drawbacks are that experienced millers have less time to teach, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate for bakery buyers.

Off-the-job training: The agricultural college course at $640 per member costs 14 × $640 = $8,960, small beside the $840,000 investment. It provides structured grain-handling skills and a recognised certificate, useful for a cooperative selling to regional bakeries. However, it takes 14 of 72 members away from the mill during processing, risking deliveries longer than 3.4 days, and generic content may not match MBG's new silos.

Decision: MBG should choose on-the-job training first, with short certified college modules later. It is cheaper, equipment-specific and avoids worsening output while 9% absenteeism already stretches a workforce of 72. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost shifts and $8,960 fee would hit the 24,600-sack operation and the generic course would not cover the new mill's exact settings. A pilot on one shift should compare the 2.1% defect rate and 6% grain loss before MBG spends $8,960 on all 14 members.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MBG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of MBG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MBG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 100,000 − ($300,000 ÷ ($21.00 − $9.00)) = 100,000 − 25,000 = 75,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 75,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate MBG's average total cost per sack.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = Fixed cost per unit + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ 100,000 units = $3.00, plus $9.00 = $12.00. Answer: average total cost is $12.00 a sack.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MBG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. A margin of safety of 75,000 sacks against output of 100,000 shows the cooperative can withstand a large drop in bakery orders and still cover $300,000 fixed costs, guiding how quickly to run the $840,000 mill.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 (from $21.00 − $9.00) lets managers test a volume discount: cutting the $21.00 price by $1 to $20.00 leaves $11.00 contribution, so they can judge whether extra orders offset the loss.
3. Average total cost of $12.00 against the $21.00 price gives a $9.00 margin a sack, a benchmark for reducing the 6% grain loss and for assessing the $0.25 premium accepted by 63% of 640 bakery buyers.
4. Managers can compare unit cost with the $640 per-member training fee and 14 untrained members to see whether cutting the 2.1% defect rate pays, and review the $9.00 variable cost given 9.4% fertiliser and transport inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Margin of safety = 75,000 units | (ii) Average total cost = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 75,000-sack cushion above break-even; $12.00 contribution for discount decisions; $12.00 unit cost versus $21.00 price and 6% loss; and $640 training spend benchmark for 14 untrained members.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MBG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MBG's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.72 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $130,000 inventories + $85,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $105,000 + $88,000 = $303,000. For 2024, $275,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.72 and ($275,000 − $130,000) ÷ $160,000 = $145,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.91. For 2025, $303,000 ÷ $155,000 = 1.95 and ($303,000 − $110,000) ÷ $155,000 = $193,000 ÷ $155,000 = 1.25.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The first ratio rose from 1.72 to 1.95 because current assets grew from $275,000 to $303,000 while current liabilities fell from $160,000 to $155,000, with cash rising from $60,000 to $88,000. The second measure climbed from 0.91 to 1.25, so MBG can now cover short-term debts without selling $110,000 of grain stock, important while $500,000 of member share capital and an $840,000 mill upgrade are being absorbed. The reservation is trade receivables, up from $85,000 to $105,000, which tie up cash if bakeries pay late, and 9% absenteeism could disrupt the 3.4-day delivery service.

Conclusion: MBG's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the gain does not rely on inventories, so short-term solvency is stronger. Higher receivables remain the main risk, so the cooperative should tighten credit control as the mill upgrade proceeds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: MBG is considering promoting its flour as locally milled on every sack. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MBG of this branding decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Labelling flour as locally milled matches the 63% of 640 bakery buyers who would pay $0.25 more and the 54% who check the origin label, supporting the $12.00 contribution per sack against 9.4% fertiliser and transport inflation. It also strengthens MBG's cooperative identity with regional bakeries and helps justify the $840,000 mill upgrade.

Disadvantage: Redesigning sacks and promoting the claim adds costs that the insert does not quantify, so the net gain cannot be calculated. If the local-origin claim is challenged, MBG's reputation with the 54% who check labels could suffer, and any delivery slip beyond the current 3.4 days would weaken the premium message. MBG should test the label with a small group of bakery buyers before a full rollout.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MBG's survey, costs and service record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.50%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in fertiliser and transport input costs will affect MBG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.50%): MBG funded the $840,000 upgrade with member shares and retained profit, so the insert identifies no bank borrowing on which to compute interest. If any future milling finance were variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point would apply to the sum borrowed; against fixed costs of $300,000 the direct effect on current operations is limited. Higher rates could still slightly slow the 3.8% growth in artisan-bread spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.66 an hour): MBG's workforce of 72 worker-members includes hourly-paid mill staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 100,000 units ÷ 72 staff = about 1,388.9 sacks per worker, so the wage rise is sustainable only if that rate holds; cutting 9% absenteeism and training the 14 untrained members would help.

Input cost inflation (9.4%): Fertiliser and transport feed the $9.00 variable cost on every sack. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $9.00 were exposed, 9.4% × $9.00 = $0.846, about $0.85 a sack, and at 100,000 units that is roughly $84,600 a year (100,000 × $0.846). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $12.00 contribution on each sack and recurs with every sale.

Conclusion: The 9.4% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats across 100,000 sacks and directly attacks the contribution that supports the $840,000 mill upgrade, whereas the interest effect on existing operations is limited and the wage rise can be offset by sustaining 1,388.9 sacks per worker. MBG should cut the 6% grain loss and seek the $0.25 local-flour premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MBG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MBG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
